title: Dead battery or bad alternator? How to check before you buy anything
summary: Two quick tests tell you which one it is. Mine turned out to be the battery.
story: Our Yukon wouldn’t start for Jen and the kids at Dairy Queen. Before I bought any parts, I ran the same two tests I always run.

steps.text: Start with the alternator. With the engine running, put a multimeter on the battery. You want about 13 to 14 volts. Mine read 14.39, so the alternator was charging fine.
If it only reads 11 or 12 volts with the engine running, suspect the alternator first. The battery might be fine.
Charge the battery, then load test it. Hook up the tester, push the button, and watch the needle. Mine dove into WEAK and didn’t come back. Official diagnosis: dead battery.
Test the new battery the same way, so you can see what a good one looks like.

title: How to fix a drill battery that won’t charge
summary: The charger can’t see a completely dead battery. A few seconds on a good one wakes it up.
story: This one has the comments to prove it. People keep writing in to say it brought their dead battery back.

steps.text: If a battery has no charge at all, the charger acts like there’s no battery there.
Connect it to a good, charged battery: negative to negative, positive to positive.
Mine took about 10 seconds. Then I put it on the charger and the charger accepted it.

caution: Use a matching battery from the same tool line, and stop right away if anything gets hot.
kitNote: Nothing to buy for this one. Those are my favorite fixes.

title: The battery tire inflator I keep in the truck
summary: I test these on real truck tires, not on a desk. The Vortex S7 is the fastest pump I’ve tested.
story: A low tire is a lot less of a problem when you’ve got a pump that can handle it. So I test them on my truck to see what they really do.

steps.text: I paid for the Vortex S7 myself and put it on a real truck tire, so you can see what it actually does.
Etenwolf sent me the smaller S1 to review. I drained a big truck tire down to 3 pounds to see if it could bring it back, and it knocked it out of the park.

title: Half my Christmas tree wouldn’t light up. One LED was the problem.
summary: A beginner soldering kit, one backwards LED, and a good lesson in tracking down what went wrong.
story: I got into soldering with these little kits. I plugged this one in and half the tree stayed dark. It works in the end, and it’s a fun little craft night project if you want to learn to solder.

steps.text: Learn to read the resistor stripes before you start.
Then solder the parts: resistors, capacitors, transistors, and LEDs.
When half of it stays dark, go looking for the backwards LED. Mine was in the wrong way around.
If a part fights you coming back out, check your iron. Turns out I’d bumped mine down to 100.

title: Flushing transmission fluid through the cooler line, mistakes included
summary: No pan drop, just a fitting and a hose. It went fine on my Silverado. Then my Yukon started slipping, so watch both first.
story: I ignored the transmission fluid on our vehicles way too long, so it was time to repent. I’m not a mechanic, just stubborn.

steps.text: I flushed my 2017 Silverado through the cooler line at the radiator, with no pan drop.
The retainer clip was the boss fight. Give yourself more time than 15 minutes.
Make sure you’re hooked to the right line. I wasn’t, and I dumped a quart on the driveway.
Use the ATF your owner’s manual calls for, then check levels the next morning.

caution: On our Yukon, the transmission started slipping on the first dinner run after the flush. Watch that video before you decide to do this.
kitNote: Plus 3/8 inch clear hose, a catch pan, and the ATF your owner’s manual calls for.

title: Boost a small air compressor with a propane tank
summary: I added an 11-gallon tank to a Husky 4.5 gallon compressor to get enough air to sandblast tractor parts.
story: A lot of you found this one on your own. I needed more air for sandblasting the tractor, so I added a second tank.

steps.text: I teed in ahead of the regulator, so the second tank fills to full pressure.
I picked a new propane tank that had never held propane, so there’s no smell to deal with.
I used a full flow fitting and Teflon tape. Watch out, propane threads are lefty tighty.
Plug in the tank side of the hose first. A pressurized hose whips around, and I’ve got the cut on my leg to prove it.
While you’re out there, purge the water from your compressor tank. Mine ran and ran.

caution: Be safe. This is not a how-to on making an old propane tank safe.
